subject: 프레스코가 벽에 스며드는 방식
title: How Pigment Enters a Wall
content: Fresco is not decoration applied onto a finished wall but pigment incorporated into the substance of the wall itself, and that distinction governs the entire craft. The painter first spreads a thin coat of wet lime plaster across the section of wall that one day of work can cover. Mineral pigment suspended in ordinary water is then carried into that receptive layer while the lime remains chemically active. As the plaster dries it draws carbon dioxide from the air and hardens into a shell of crystal. The color becomes embedded within that structure rather than resting upon the surface, which explains why the imagery resists removal. This binding gives the method its long life span, yet the same chemistry makes it unforgiving. The available interval is severely limited, because plaster beginning to harden will no longer accept additional pigment. A painter therefore has to divide the design into daily patches and finish each one before the light fails. The junctions between adjacent sections remain visible to any observer examining the surface obliquely. They record the order of work as clearly as a diary, and they cannot be hidden by later retouching. Corrections require removing hardened material and replastering, meaning a miscalculation destroys an entire section rather than a single stroke. For this reason the design was fixed in advance through drawings scaled to the wall itself. Certain pigments were additionally prohibited, since intense blues and greens deteriorated in alkaline conditions and required application in organic binders afterward. Those added passages aged at a different rate, and in many old rooms the sky has faded while the ground has not. What endures today constitutes an incomplete record, determined by material chemistry as decisively as by artistic intention. Reading such a wall means reading two histories at once, one of intention and one of material.

subject: 캔버스가 목판을 대체한 경위
title: Why Canvas Replaced the Panel
content: For several centuries a serious European painting was executed on wooden panel, and the eventual transition to woven fabric altered considerably more than the surface. A panel had to be cut from a single seasoned plank, planed flat, and sealed with layers of chalk ground before any color touched it. That preparation was laborious and expensive, and the completed object remained heavy enough to attach a picture permanently to its intended interior. Wood also moved with the weather, so panels split along the grain and lifted their paint in dry air. Fabric stretched across a lightweight framework resolved several of these difficulties simultaneously, and it resolved them inexpensively. A canvas could be made in almost any size by sewing widths together, which freed painters from the width of a tree. It weighed a fraction of an equivalent panel, so an enormous picture could travel by wagon or by merchant vessel. It could even be rolled for the journey and stretched again at the far end, and dealers were quick to see what that allowed. The commercial market consequently expanded, since a painting produced in one city became available in another. The change also altered how paint behaved on the surface, because woven cloth has a texture that wood does not. Brushwork appearing insubstantial on a smooth panel acquired considerable presence when it caught the projecting weave. Painters began to leave the marks of the brush visible rather than polishing them away. Certain critics interpreted this looseness as negligence, yet within a generation it became an acknowledged demonstration of skill. The new support had its own weaknesses, for cloth slackens, tears, and rots in damp rooms. Restorers still devote much of their labor to repairing damage that a wooden panel would never have suffered. The trade accepted that cost because mobility mattered more to the people buying pictures than permanence did.

subject: 금박이 성상화에서 한 역할
title: Gold in the Sacred Image
content: Gold leaf within a devotional panel is frequently described as ornament, although it functioned as an explicit statement about pictorial space. Behind the painted figures the ground was not sky, landscape, or room; it was a flat sheet of beaten metal. That surface categorically refuses depth, and it advances the figures toward the physical space occupied by the worshipper. A painter who used it was therefore saying that the scene does not belong to the ordinary world at all. The material additionally behaves in ways no pigment can imitate, and this behavior constituted much of its significance. Gold reflects whatever light falls on it, so the image changes as a candle moves or a door opens. Within a darkened church the background appears to breathe, and the figures seem to emerge from a continually shifting radiance. No pigment of the time could produce that effect, since paint absorbs light instead of returning it. The leaf was beaten sufficiently thin that a single coin might cover an entire panel, making the display considerably less expensive than it appeared. Even so the material carried a clear price, and donors knew what they were paying for. Surviving contracts frequently specify the weight of gold before they specify the subject of the commission. When painters later learned to build convincing depth with color alone, the gold ground began to look old. It was superseded by blue skies and distant hills, and the sacred narrative entered a world resembling our own. Some scholars read that change as progress toward realism, yet it also gave up something specific. A painted sky becomes permanently fixed once the varnish dries, whereas a golden background responds to every lamp carried near it. The older panels were made for rooms lit by flame rather than by even daylight. Displayed beneath a modern gallery fixture, they forfeit the precise quality that originally made them overwhelming.

subject: 밑그림이 완성작에 남긴 흔적
title: What the Underdrawing Records
content: Infrared photography has demonstrated that numerous finished paintings rest upon preparatory drawings no viewer was ever intended to see. The pigments used in a final layer are often transparent to infrared light, while the black chalk beneath is not. A camera recording that band therefore penetrates the color and discovers the underlying plan that directed it. What appears is rarely a neat copy of the surface, and the differences are the point. Arms are repositioned, heads rotate in the opposite direction, and complete figures occupy areas containing nothing but shadow. Such changes tell us that the design was argued out on the panel itself rather than settled in advance. This discovery overturned a durable assumption concerning how earlier pictures were actually manufactured. Writers had assumed that a master worked from a fixed cartoon and that the painting was mere execution. The evidence instead reveals a procedure of experiment, throughout which the picture was continually revised while developing. It also helps separate hands within a workshop, because a copy tends to lack these second thoughts. An apprentice following a model draws once and paints once, since no compositional problem remains for solving. When a panel shows a confident line abandoned for a better one, the maker was inventing rather than repeating. Attributions have been quietly rewritten upon exactly this basis in numerous major collections. The method has limits that its users are careful to state, for some grounds block the beam entirely. Chalk drawings register clearly whereas metal point frequently does not, and a dense white layer conceals everything beneath. A blank result is thus not proof that no drawing exists, only that none can be seen. Interpreted with appropriate caution, these images have reopened a stage of production that remained inaccessible for centuries.

subject: 데생과 소묘의 위계
title: Drawing and the Order of Value
content: Within most European academies drawing was ranked above color, and that hierarchy was defended explicitly as a question of intellect. A line, the argument ran, comes from the mind and states what a thing is. Color merely reports how an object happens to appear beneath one illumination on one afternoon. Students therefore spent years on chalk and paper before they were allowed to touch oil. They copied engravings, subsequently plaster casts of celebrated statues, and only afterward the living model. The order was strict, and it shaped what the finished pictures were expected to say. This hierarchy protected the social standing of painters quite as much as the quality of their production. If painting was an art of the mind, it belonged with poetry rather than with the crafts. Guild members grinding pigment and gilding frames could then be assigned a demonstrably inferior position. The academy defended a border, and drawing was the wall it built along that border. Opposing this position stood painters maintaining that color carried the essential truth of vision. They pointed out that no edge in nature is a line, and that a line is already a fiction. Drawing an outline means deciding where an object terminates, which the unaided eye never accomplishes so cleanly. The argument ran for two centuries and was never settled by evidence, since it was never really about evidence. It concluded when the training sustaining it disintegrated, and the institutions ranking these skills forfeited their authority. Studios now teach both at once, and the old sequence survives mainly as a habit of speech. We continue calling a preliminary plan a drawing and a completed object a painting, as though the second necessarily follows the first. That habit hides how often the two have been done with one gesture.

subject: 삼면 제단화의 서사 배치
title: Telling a Story Across Three Panels
content: An altarpiece equipped with hinged wings functions as a mechanism for narrating a story across more than one condition. Closed, it shows a sober outer face, usually painted in muted grays that imitate carved stone. Opened, it discloses a luminous center flanked by two subordinate scenes conducting the eye inward. The object thus has at least two appearances, and the church calendar decided which one the congregation saw. Throughout ordinary weekdays the wings remained closed, and the complete image was reserved exclusively for festivals. This design solved a problem that a single picture cannot solve. A narrative contains a before and an afterward, whereas a painted surface accommodates only one instant. By splitting the surface, the maker could set an early event beside a late one without confusing them. The framing between panels performs precisely the function that a paragraph division performs in writing. Viewers learned to read left to right across the wings and to treat the center as the claim that the wings support. The arrangement additionally encoded rank, since dimension and position carried significance requiring no explanatory label. The largest figure stood in the middle, and the donors who paid for the work knelt at the edges. Their scale was diminished, and they appeared frequently in profile rather than confronting the congregation directly. Nobody had to explain this, because the grammar was shared by everyone in the room. Museums have dismantled most of these objects, and the individual panels presently hang as independent pictures. A wing may be in one country while its center is in another, and both are labeled as independent works. What disappears is not merely the sequence but the hinge itself, the circumstance that the object could transform. A visitor sees a still image where the original audience saw an object that opened and closed.

subject: 부조와 환조 사이의 선택
title: Choosing Between Relief and the Round
content: A sculptor choosing between relief and freestanding work is essentially deciding how thoroughly the viewer should be controlled. A figure carved in the round can be walked around, and every angle becomes part of the work. That freedom constitutes a burden equally, since the maker must resolve the form from directions nobody may ever occupy. Relief keeps the image attached to its ground and fixes the range of views to a narrow band. Within that restricted band the sculptor may employ devices that a freestanding figure would immediately expose. Depth in relief is often a matter of suggestion rather than of actual thickness. A carver might cut the nearer figures merely a finger deep and still persuade us they stand well forward. Lines can be compressed, and heads that should be far apart can be stacked with no loss of sense. Painters employ comparable devices, so relief occupies a position between the two arts rather than belonging entirely to either. The choice therefore depends on where the work will be seen and how long anyone will stand there. Relief additionally survives architectural exposure better, because it shares the supporting mass of the wall carrying it. A free standing figure on a high ledge is a weight held out over the street, and it needs anchors that may fail. Wind, frost, and accumulated snow all operate more destructively upon a form possessing open extended limbs. Many of the figures we admire in the round were made for niches that protected them on three sides. The distinction has softened considerably in recent practice, where sculptors permit a piece to remain partially attached. That middle state was once a compromise, and it is now often the point. What both traditions genuinely share is a single constraint, namely that removed stone can never be restored.

subject: 대리석 결이 조각가에게 준 제약
title: What the Grain of Marble Allows
content: Marble looks uniform from a distance, yet every block carries a hidden structure that the carver must respect. The stone was once limestone, and heat and pressure recrystallized it into interlocking grains. Those grains have a preferred direction, and a chisel driven across it behaves differently from one driven along it. A sculptor who ignores this loses a hand or a wing to a split that follows the bedding plane. Ancient workshops therefore quarried with the finished pose already in mind. Thin projecting parts were the first problem, since an arm held free of the body is a lever on a brittle material. Roman copies of Greek bronzes solved it with struts and tree trunks that had no place in the original. Those supports are often read as clumsy additions, but they are the honest cost of a change in material. A bronze arm can reach out because metal has tensile strength, while stone has almost none. The same pose in marble needs help, and the help has to stand somewhere in the design. Color and flaw set further limits that no amount of skill removes. A vein running through a block may be invisible on the outer face and appear only when carving reaches it. Work that has taken months can be ruined in an hour by a fault the quarry could not see. Contracts from several periods therefore assign that risk explicitly to one party or the other. The best carvers used such accidents rather than fighting them, letting a gray streak fall across a garment. Sculptors today can choose materials that behave more predictably, and many still return to this one. The reason is not tradition alone but the way light enters the surface and scatters a short way inside. That slight glow is why marble skin has never been matched by cast substitutes.

subject: 석고 본이 만든 복제의 문화
title: Casts and a Culture of Copies
content: Before photography, plaster casts were how the world saw the famous statues it could not visit. A mold taken from an original could yield an unlimited run of copies at a modest price. Schools bought them by the crate, and students drew from them for years before meeting a live model. Whole museums were built for casts alone, and their halls held works from cities a month of travel apart. Such rooms made comparison possible in a way that no set of engravings could match. The copies were not treated as inferior objects, and that attitude is easy to misread today. What mattered to their users was the form, which the cast reproduced with mechanical accuracy. Surface color, tool marks, and the history of the stone were all considered accidents of the individual block. A cast therefore gave the essential work and stripped away what was merely local. This reasoning fits a period that believed a statue was above all a design. Attitudes changed when the original object came to be valued as a unique historical thing. Casts then looked like ghosts, and many collections dumped them in cellars or broke them up. Some of those discarded plasters have since become evidence, because the originals have weathered badly since the mold was taken. A cast made in the last century can record a face that acid rain has now erased. Conservators consult them as a form of documentation rather than as art. The reversal is a useful reminder that the line between copy and record is drawn by need. Nothing about the plaster changed, and only the questions asked of it did. Institutions are now rebuilding cast halls they once emptied, and the rebuilding is defended in the language of archives.

subject: 기념비의 규모와 정치
title: Scale and the Politics of Monuments
content: A monument makes its argument through size before anyone reads a word of the inscription. Height forces the viewer to look up, and looking up is a posture with a long history of meaning. Width blocks a sightline and takes possession of the ground it occupies. These effects work on people who know nothing about the person being honored. Sponsors have understood this for as long as public sculpture has existed. The relation between scale and cost also matters, because a large work announces the resources behind it. A city that raises a figure three times life size is stating what it can afford to spend. Rivals read that statement clearly, and answering monuments often appear within a few years. Sequences of this kind can be traced in many capitals, where each generation built slightly larger than the last. The escalation stops only when the site runs out of room or the money runs out first. Scale further decides how a monument ages, since a small work can be moved and a huge one usually cannot. When the politics that produced a figure fall out of favor, the removal becomes an engineering problem. Cranes, road closures, and structural surveys turn a symbolic act into a costly public event. That difficulty has often preserved statues that few people would now choose to raise. Some cities have answered by leaving the object and changing its setting instead. New plaques, altered lighting, and works placed nearby can shift what a monument says without touching it. This approach treats the site as a conversation rather than a verdict. It also concedes that scale, once built, is very hard to argue with directly.

subject: 정원 설계가 다룬 시선의 축
title: The Axis a Garden Builds
content: A formal garden is less a collection of plants than a design for where the eye is allowed to go. The long central path is the clearest device, since it draws the gaze to a single distant point. Everything set along that line gains importance, and everything off it becomes a wing. Visitors follow the axis without being told to, because open ground reads as an invitation. Control of movement is thus achieved by shape alone rather than by walls or signs. The device also manages what the visitor cannot see, which is often the more important half. Hedges at the right height hide the working parts of an estate while leaving the horizon open. A slope can be cut so that a wall vanishes from view and the lawn appears to continue into farmland. Such a hidden ditch lets cattle be kept out without any visible barrier interrupting the scene. The owner then appears to possess the whole landscape, including land that belongs to somebody else. Gardens in other traditions reversed the logic and denied the long view on purpose. Paths were made to bend so that the destination stayed hidden until the last few steps. Each turn offered a composed scene, and the walker met a sequence rather than a single picture. Time became part of the design, since the garden could not be grasped from any one position. Neither approach is more natural, and both are arguments about how a person should be led. The straight axis says that order can be seen whole from the right place. The winding path says that understanding arrives in pieces and only to those who walk.

subject: 탑의 층수와 상징 체계
title: Counting the Stories of a Pagoda
content: The tiers of a pagoda look like floors, yet in most examples nobody could ever stand on them. The interior is often solid or holds only a narrow shaft with a ladder. What the eye reads as architecture is therefore closer to sculpture built at the scale of a building. Understanding the form requires asking what the tiers were meant to count rather than to hold. The answer lies in a relic mound and in the umbrellas raised above it as a mark of honor. Early Indian structures placed a stack of discs on a dome to signal rank, and that stack traveled east. As it moved, local builders translated it into the timber roofs they already knew how to make. Each disc became a story with eaves, and the mound below became a base or vanished entirely. The result kept the numerical logic of the original while looking like a familiar tower. Odd numbers were preferred throughout, and that preference survived every change of material. Height was limited by the same problem that limits any tall timber frame, namely the wind. Builders answered with a central pillar that hangs rather than carries, acting as a heavy pendulum. When the frame sways, this mass moves out of phase and damps the motion instead of adding to it. Several structures with such pillars have stood through earthquakes that flattened stone buildings nearby. Engineers studying them have borrowed the principle for towers that have no religious purpose at all. The lesson is that a form driven by symbolism can still solve a physical problem well. Symbol and structure were never separate departments for the people who built these towers.

subject: 아치가 벽을 열어 준 방식
title: What an Arch Opens
content: A masonry wall performs superbly in compression and becomes helpless the moment an opening is cut through it. Placing a flat beam across the gap solves the problem only for short spans, since stone snaps under bending. The arch responds by converting the opening into a curve where every component is compressed instead of bent. Each wedge pushes on its neighbors, and the whole line of thrust travels down to the ground. Because masonry resists compression exceptionally well, an arch spans considerably more than any lintel of identical material. That geometry has consequences the builder cannot avoid. The thrust does not descend vertically but leans outward at the springing of the curve. Something must resist that push, whether a thick wall, a buttress, or a second arch leaning back the other way. Sequences of arches therefore require heavy terminal supports even when the intervening bays appear weightless. Many collapses in old buildings begin at the last bay of an arcade, where nothing pushes back. Construction demands temporary support additionally, since an arch cannot stand until the concluding wedge is positioned. Carpenters built a wooden form to hold the wedges in place while the ring was closed. Removing that centering constituted the decisive moment, and it proceeded gradually through wedges and boxes of sand. The timber often cost more than the stone, and it could be reused only a few times. This concealed expenditure determined how many openings a project could afford and how uniform they became. Repetition was cheap because one form served many openings, and variety was costly. Much of what we interpret as a stylistic preference for regular arcades originated as an economy of scaffolding.

subject: 창호가 빛을 다루는 방법
title: Windows and the Handling of Light
content: A window is usually described as a hole for light, but every tradition treats it as a filter. Size, height, and covering all decide how much light enters and what it does once inside. Direct sun makes strong shadows and hard contrast, which suits some rooms and ruins others. A surface that scatters the beam turns the same sun into an even glow with no sharp edge. Builders have chosen between these effects for as long as they have cut openings in walls. Paper screens in East Asian houses take the second path deliberately. The fibers spread incoming light across the whole panel, so the room brightens without a single bright spot. Because the paper is thin, the level indoors follows the sky closely and changes through the day. Rooms lit this way feel calm, and the flatness suits interiors where the floor is the main surface. The same screens give almost no view, which was accepted as part of the arrangement. European glazing made the opposite trade and kept the view at the cost of glare. Clear glass admits both the light and the image of what lies outside, which is why shutters and curtains multiplied. Deep reveals, small panes, and colored glass were all ways of softening what plain glazing let in. A cathedral window is the extreme case, since it converts light into color before releasing it. The wall then becomes a source rather than an opening, and the outside world disappears. Modern buildings have returned to large clear panes and now spend heavily on blinds and coatings. The problem has not changed at all, and only the materials used to manage it have.

subject: 초가와 기와의 재료 논리
title: The Logic of Thatch and Tile
content: Roofing decisions appear to be matters of taste until the available local materials are taken into account. Thatch is made from straw or reed that a farming settlement already produces every year. It costs labor instead of currency, and that labor can be distributed among neighbors during an unoccupied season. Tile requires clay, a kiln, fuel, and a maker who does nothing else, which implies a market and a town. The two roofing systems therefore indicate different economies before they indicate different preferences. Their physical behavior differs just as sharply, and each has a matching structure below. Thatch is remarkably light, so the supporting frame can remain slender and the walls comparatively thin. It insulates well because the layer traps a great deal of still air within the stems. It must be pitched steeply to discharge water rapidly, and it requires renewal every several decades. Fire is the standing danger, and whole villages were lost to a single spark on a dry night. Tile is heavy and demands a frame sufficiently strong to carry several times the burden of thatch. That weight is also an advantage, since tiles resist wind and need no ridge rope to hold them down. They survive for generations with nothing beyond localized repairs, and they cannot burn. The cost appears at the start rather than through the life of the building, which favors owners with capital. Interpreting a roof as an indication of wealth is therefore reasonable, although the reasoning is frequently stated too simply. A thatched house in a region with no clay says nothing about the means of the family inside. Materials testify about location first, and only subsequently about the finances of the builder.

subject: 목조 결구의 이음 방식
title: Joints in a Timber Frame
content: A timber building holds together at its joints, and the way those joints are cut reveals a whole tradition. Where iron was scarce or costly, carpenters shaped wood so that the pieces locked without any nails. A tenon cut on one member enters a mortise cut in another, and a wooden pin holds the pair. The pin is often set slightly off center so that driving it pulls the joint tight. Such details are invisible once the frame is raised, yet they decide whether the building survives a century. Joints of this kind behave differently from bolted or welded connections in one important way. They allow small movements, and that slight looseness lets a frame absorb shaking instead of resisting it. During a tremor the members shift, rub, and return, and the friction turns motion into heat. A rigid connection concentrates force at a single point until something breaks there. Traditional frames in earthquake regions have survived shocks that stiffer structures did not. The system imposes its own costs, since every joint must be cut to fit its particular pair of timbers. Members are not interchangeable, and a replacement has to be shaped on site by a skilled hand. Repair therefore requires the same knowledge as construction, which is why the loss of that knowledge dooms old buildings. Several countries now train carpenters specifically to maintain frames that nobody would build from scratch. The training is expensive and is defended as heritage rather than as economy. Engineers have begun studying these joints for reasons that have nothing to do with heritage. A connection that yields a little and then recovers is exactly what a modern seismic design wants.

subject: 탈의 조형과 배역
title: Masks and the Fixing of a Role
content: A mask removes the face of the performer and replaces it with a fixed expression that cannot change. This looks like a loss, and traditions that use masks treat it as the opposite. Because the face is settled, everything else must carry the meaning, and the body takes over the work. The angle of the head, the speed of a step, and the tilt of a shoulder become legible at a distance. In an open theater holding thousands, that legibility was a practical necessity rather than a style. The fixed face also carries an advantage that a live face cannot. A mask read under changing light appears to shift, since a slight tilt alters every shadow on it. Skilled performers exploit this and can make a carved smile seem to darken by lowering the chin. Audiences describe the mask as changing, and in a strict sense they are reporting the truth about the light. The carver builds this possibility in by keeping the surfaces subtly curved rather than flat. Masks further allow a role to outlive the person playing it, and this is why they suit repertory traditions. The character belongs to the company rather than to any actor, and the same object may be worn for generations. Wear on the inside records the succession of faces that have pressed against it. Some troupes treat the older masks as too valuable to use and commission copies for performance. That decision preserves the object and breaks the chain that gave it meaning. Modern directors sometimes borrow masks for productions in traditions that never used them. The results often fail, because the surrounding grammar of movement is missing and the face simply looks blank.

subject: 무대 장치의 전환 기술
title: Changing the Scene in View
content: Every theater must answer a single question about scene changes, namely whether the audience ought to witness them. Concealing the change requires a curtain, a darkened stage, or machinery operating beneath the floorboards, and each of those solutions costs money. Revealing it requires the opposite decision, that the mechanics themselves form part of what the audience actually came to see. Both answers possess long histories in the theater, and neither one is a technical default that follows from the building. The choice tells us what a particular tradition believes a performance fundamentally is. Baroque stages travelled remarkably far toward concealment and constructed astonishing machines in order to achieve it. Painted flats ran in grooves and could be withdrawn simultaneously by a system of ropes and drums installed below the stage. A single crank turned those drums and moved every wing at the same instant, so that a forest became a palace between two beats of the music. The whole effect depended upon the change happening faster than an audience could possibly follow it. Spectators were meant to experience a transformation rather than to watch a crew of men doing their work. Other traditions have made the crew entirely visible and even dressed them in a color that means please ignore this person. Assistants hand properties to the actors in full view of the house, and the convention is accepted without the slightest difficulty. Once an audience has agreed to look past a figure, that figure is free to do useful work in the open. This arrangement costs nothing in machinery and requires only a shared rule between the stage and the people watching it. The rule is learned very quickly, which is why visitors from other traditions adapt to it within a single act. Contemporary staging frequently mixes both approaches inside one production. A change may be concealed when the story requires surprise and exposed when the same story requires distance.

subject: 인형극의 조종 방식
title: How a Puppet Is Driven
content: Puppet traditions differ most in where the control sits, and that difference shapes what the figures can express. Strings from above allow walking, jumping, and the loose swing of a limb that suggests weight. Rods from below give firmer control of the arms and let a figure hold a pose without drift. A hand inside the body gives the fastest response of all and the smallest range of gesture. Each method is good at something the others do badly, and no tradition has combined them all successfully. String figures excel at the illusion of gravity because the limbs really do hang and swing. An operator releases tension and the leg falls on its own, which no motor imitates convincingly. The cost is precision, since every string is long and the figure lags behind the hand that moves it. Fine work such as picking up a small object is slow and often avoided in the writing. Repertoires therefore favor scenes of travel, dance, and combat where the swing itself carries the meaning. Rod puppets reverse the trade and are used where the story needs deliberate handling of objects. The arms respond immediately, and the operator can hold a gesture for as long as a speech requires. Because the rods come from below, the stage must hide the operator behind a screen or a low wall. That requirement fixes the sightlines and explains why such theaters look alike across distant regions. Three operators may work a single large figure, with one on the head and one on each arm. Their training is measured in years, and the junior positions are held for a decade before promotion. The hierarchy is often described as ceremony, though it is mostly the time needed to learn a shared rhythm.

subject: 가부키의 정형 동작
title: Fixed Forms in Kabuki
content: Certain moments in Kabuki freeze, and the actor holds a pose while the music strikes a wooden block. This device is not a pause in the action but a statement that the action has reached a peak. The pose gathers the meaning of a scene into one shape that the audience can hold in memory. Prints sold outside the theater reproduced these shapes, and playgoers recognized them at once. The image and the performance therefore supported each other in a way that few traditions match. The convention rewards repetition rather than novelty, which is easy to misread from outside. A spectator familiar with the form is not waiting to learn what happens next in the plot. The stories are known, and the interest lies in how a particular actor realizes a known moment. Small variations in timing and weight carry the whole judgment of a performance. Criticism in this setting is comparative by nature, since every version is measured against remembered ones. Family lines reinforce that comparison because roles and names pass from one generation to the next. An actor may take a stage name held by his predecessors and be judged against all of them. This structure gives the audience a long memory and gives the performer a heavy inheritance. It also concentrates authority, since the right to certain roles is not open to everyone. Reformers have attacked the arrangement repeatedly and have changed less than they hoped. The system survives because the comparative pleasure it produces depends on exactly this continuity. Break the line and the audience loses the standard against which the evening is measured.

subject: 발레의 발 위치 체계
title: Five Positions and a Vocabulary
content: Classical ballet begins from five positions of the feet, and those positions are more than a starting exercise. Each turns the leg outward from the hip so that the knee and the foot point away from the body. This rotation is the foundation of the whole technique, and everything else is built on top of it. It widens the base, allows movement in any direction without a preparatory turn, and presents a clean line to the front. The dancer therefore faces the audience while traveling sideways, which a natural stance makes impossible. The system was written down at a court where dance and etiquette overlapped completely. Ranked positions made steps teachable in words, and a notation could then record a dance for absent performers. Once a vocabulary existed, choreography could be composed like music from named units. Teachers in different cities could produce dancers who were able to work together on first meeting. That portability is why the vocabulary spread while other court dances vanished with their courts. The cost of the system falls on the body and is paid over a career. Turnout that exceeds the natural range of the hip is often forced from the knee and the ankle instead. Injury patterns in ballet dancers cluster exactly where that compensation happens. Training now works to develop rotation slowly rather than to demand it immediately from children. The change came from medicine rather than from any argument inside the art. Some contemporary choreographers reject the positions entirely and build movement from ordinary walking. Their work still depends on the older vocabulary, because it is legible mainly as a refusal of it.

subject: 탈춤의 풍자 관습
title: Satire in the Masked Dance
content: Village masked dance in Korea worked as licensed criticism, and the license was the whole point. Performers wore exaggerated faces representing a corrupt monk, a foolish aristocrat, and a servant who outwits both. Under a mask the speaker had no identity, so words that would be punished in daily life could be said aloud. The audience stood in a ring rather than in seats, and it answered the performers directly. That arrangement made the event a conversation with a script rather than a show delivered to silent viewers. The targets were chosen with care, and the pattern reveals the limits of the freedom. Local officials, landlords, and clergy appeared constantly, while the throne did not. Criticism ran upward only as far as the people the village actually dealt with. This is a common shape for permitted satire in many societies, and it is not a failure of nerve. A form that attacked everything would have been suppressed and would have stopped existing. Timing mattered as much as content, since the performances belonged to festival days set in the calendar. On those days the ordinary rules were relaxed by agreement, and everyone knew when the license ended. The suspension was bounded, and that boundary is what made it tolerable to those in charge. Scholars disagree about whether such release strengthened the existing order or weakened it. The evidence supports both readings, and it probably differed from one village to the next. What is clear is that the form declined when the audience stopped standing in that ring. Moved onto a stage and preserved as heritage, the dance kept its steps and lost its argument.

subject: 안무의 저작 개념
title: Who Owns a Sequence of Steps
content: Choreography remained outside copyright protection for a long time, and the reason was a stubborn problem of record. Most legal systems protect creative works that have been fixed in some material form that another person can examine. A novel exists on paper, and a song can be written down in notation, but a dance disappears at the instant it is performed. Without a stable record there was simply nothing for the law to point at, compare, and rule upon. Dancers therefore relied on custom, reputation, and private contracts rather than on any statute. Notation systems were invented repeatedly to close this gap, and not one of them was ever widely adopted. Each required years of training, and a written score took far more time to produce than the dance itself took to teach. Companies found it much cheaper to keep the work stored in the bodies of the dancers who performed it. Knowledge passed from a retiring performer to a younger one in the studio, with corrections given by hand and by demonstration. That method transmits detail no notation has ever captured and loses absolutely everything when the chain is broken. Film changed the legal situation far more decisively than any notation system ever managed to. A recording is a fixed form, and courts in several countries accepted it as sufficient for the purposes of protection. Choreographers gained the ability to license their work and to object whenever it was copied without their permission. The change also created a difficult new question about what exactly is protected within the recording. A camera captures one performance, including the accidents of that night and the particular qualities of those dancers. Courts have therefore had to decide how much variation still counts as the very same work. Their answers borrow from music, where a piece survives many interpretations, and the borrowed reasoning fits imperfectly.

subject: 조율 체계가 만든 음색
title: Tuning Systems and the Color of Sound
content: A tuning system is a compromise, and every musical culture has chosen a different place to make it. Simple ratios between frequencies produce intervals that sound smooth and stable to almost everyone. Unfortunately these ratios cannot be stacked to close a circle, and a small gap always remains. Twelve perfect fifths do not equal seven octaves, and the difference has to be put somewhere. Where a culture puts it determines what its music can and cannot do. One answer keeps a few keys pure and pushes the whole error into the keys that are rarely used. Music written under this scheme gains real color, since each key has a distinct character. A piece in one key genuinely sounds different from the same piece moved up a step. Composers exploited those differences and chose keys for their quality rather than for the convenience of players. The price is that distant keys are unusable, and modulation is restricted to a small neighborhood. The other answer spreads the error evenly so that every interval is slightly wrong and none is unbearable. This allows free movement through all keys and makes instruments interchangeable across a whole orchestra. What disappears is the individual color of each key, since all keys are now identical in structure. Musicians of the period noticed the loss and argued about it for decades before accepting the trade. The debate is usually presented as progress toward a better system, which understates what was given up. Ensembles playing older music now often return to the earlier tunings on purpose. Listeners report hearing harmonic tension that even tuning had quietly smoothed away.
